newsitem.title: USA: Ill. House expanded gaming bill seen not passing.
newsitem.headline: Ill. House expanded gaming bill seen not passing.

text.p: An Illinois state representative said Tuesday his proposal to expand gaming in the state to partly fund $10 billion of bonds for school construction and nearly $800 million in property tax relief cannot pass this session as written.

Rep. Lou Lang, D-Skokie, said, however, that while he cannot make up the three votes he said he needs to pass the proposal by the House deadline Friday, he hopes the General Assembly will adopt part of it this year.
"Rather than withdrawing the bill, which I think is too strong a word, I have just simply indicated that I do not today have the 60 votes needed to pass the bill," Lang said Tuesday.
Lang said he hopes to convince Gov. Jim Edgar to discuss the possibility with him. Edgar has said that he opposes expanding gambling in Illinois.
But beyond gambling expansion and economic development issues, the state must create a comprehensive gaming policy, Lang said.
Lang said he had 57 votes supporting the proposal, and he never expected the bill as drafted to reach the governor.

"It's a comprehensive bill dealing with every open gaming issue and also dealing with a game plan for what to do with the revenue created," Lang said. "I'm proud of what I have done, the votes just aren't there today."

Lang estimated that expanded gambling could generate up to $1.4 billion in new revenues that would support issuing up to $1 billion of bonds for each of the next five years to be matched with local funds.

The bill proposed to add 14 new casino gaming licenses, including five for the City of Chicago and four for neighboring Rosemont. It would also have allowed dockside gaming aboard the state's riverboats and restructured gaming tax rates.
On Monday, a government watchdog group reported that gambling interests contributed $696,627 to Illinois legislative leaders, top state officials and state political parties in the last half of 1996.
The Public Access Project also reported that gambling businesses and their owners contributed more than $1.7 million in the last two years.
